overview: Dracunculiasis, also called Guinea-worm disease, is a parasitic disease transmitted through contaminated drinking water, causing a painful blister from which a worm slowly emerges. It results from ingesting the parasite Dracunculus medinensis. Although it rarely causes death, infected individuals are often incapacitated for weeks or months.
symptoms: Painful blister on the lower leg
transmission: Drinking stagnant water contaminated by parasite-infected water fleas
Consuming raw or undercooked aquatic hosts harbouring the infective larvae
Ingestion of infected water fleas by people and certain animals
prevention: Regularly applying temephos (Abate) to stagnant water
Community education on early case detection and reporting
Proper management of aquatic animals' waste
risk_factors: Consuming raw or undercooked aquatic hosts
key_facts: 10–14 months for the transmission cycle to complete
20 countries were endemic in the mid-1980s
5 countries – Angola, Chad, Ethiopia, Mali, and South Sudan – remain endemic
